intro/hello: Welcome to D L twenty six: deep learning, a decade later.
intro/where: C S two thirty one N taught the field as it stood in the winter of twenty sixteen.
intro/old: Images went through ConvNets, text through recurrent networks, and every task got its own model.
intro/since: In the ten years since, three shifts changed the shape of the field.
intro/arch: First, one architecture for everything: the transformer, built on attention.
intro/scale: Second, scale became a research direction: models pretrained on trillions of words.
intro/feedback: Third, models are finished by feedback: people comparing answers, and then programs checking them.
intro/same: And underneath all three, most of the code is what you already know.
intro/plan: Here is the story of that decade, and the map of the course that follows it.
decade/start: Here is the whole decade. Each dot is a milestone, colored by its thread.
decade/y17: Twenty seventeen: the Transformer. Attention replaces recurrence.
decade/y18: Twenty eighteen: G P T and BERT pretrain transformers on plain text.
decade/y19: Twenty nineteen: G P T two starts doing tasks from a prompt alone.
decade/y20: Twenty twenty is crowded: G P T three, scaling laws, the vision transformer and diffusion.
decade/y21: Twenty twenty one: clip puts pictures and words in one space, and lora makes fine-tuning cheap.
decade/y22: Twenty twenty two is the year of the assistant: Chinchilla, human feedback in Instruct G P T, and in November, Chat G P T.
decade/y23: Twenty twenty three: open weights with llama, and D P O, a simpler way to learn from preferences.
decade/y24: Twenty twenty four: rewards a program can check, G R P O, and oh one, which thinks before it answers.
decade/y25: Twenty twenty five: DeepSeek R one publishes a reasoning recipe in the open.
decade/threads: Three threads run through it all: attention, scale and feedback. Let's take them in turn.
attention/rnn: In twenty sixteen, text went through a recurrent network: one token at a time, each folded into a hidden state.
attention/slow: That is slow: a G P U wants thousands of multiplications at once, but each step waits for the one before.
attention/far: And for the last word to use the first, the information has to survive every step in between.
attention/paper: In twenty seventeen, a team at Google published Attention Is All You Need, and threw the recurrence away.
attention/all: Every token scores every other token in one matrix multiply, and all positions are computed together.
attention/block: Add a small network for each token, residual connections and normalization, and you have the Transformer block.
attention/faster: It trained in a fraction of the time of the recurrent translators, and translated better.
attention/spread: Within a year it was being pretrained on plain text. By twenty twenty, it was reading images.
softmax/know: Here is the surprise: at the heart of attention is an operation you wrote in C S two thirty one N.
softmax/cls: A linear classifier compares an input with each row of a weight matrix: one dot product, one score, per class.
softmax/soft: A softmax turns those scores into probabilities that add up to one.
softmax/att: Attention is the same line. The rows become keys, one per token, and the input becomes a query.
softmax/sqrt: Divide by the square root of the width, then apply the very same softmax.
softmax/out: What changes is the job: the weights no longer name a class, they mix the tokens' values into a new vector.
softmax/keys: And the keys are computed from the sentence itself, so the classes change with every input.
images/conv: A ConvNet has assumptions built in: nearby pixels belong together, and a cat is a cat wherever it appears.
images/vit: In twenty twenty, the vision transformer dropped them. Cut the image into sixteen by sixteen patches, each one a token.
images/data: It has to learn what a ConvNet is given, so it needs more data. With enough, it matched the best ConvNets.
images/same: Now text and images go through the same block.
images/clip: In twenty twenty one, clip trained an image encoder and a text encoder together, so a photo and its caption land close together.
images/zero: Then you can classify a photo by comparing it with sentences, like a photo of a dog.
images/shared: One architecture for many kinds of data. And when everything is a transformer, every improvement is shared.
pretrain/labels: In twenty sixteen, more data meant more labels, and labels cost money. ImageNet took years of crowd work.
pretrain/free: Text labels itself. Hide the next word of any sentence, and ask the model to predict it.
pretrain/every: Every position of every document is a training example, with its answer attached.
pretrain/loss: And the loss is the one from Assignment one: softmax cross-entropy, with the whole vocabulary as the classes.
pretrain/gpt2: G P T two, in twenty nineteen, had one and a half billion parameters, and could attempt tasks from a prompt alone.
pretrain/gpt3: G P T three, in twenty twenty, had a hundred and seventy five billion. Show it a few examples, and it continues the pattern.
pretrain/icl: No gradient step at all. It is called in-context learning.
laws/kaplan: Also in twenty twenty, Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI measured how the loss falls as models grow.
laws/law: Against parameters, data or compute, it follows a power law: a straight line on log axes.
laws/plan: That turned scale into a plan. Train small models, fit the line, and predict where a big one will land.
laws/six: The budget is one line of arithmetic: about six operations per parameter, per training token.
laws/gpt3: For G P T three, that comes to about three times ten to the twenty third operations.
laws/chin: In twenty twenty two, Chinchilla showed how to spend it: grow parameters and tokens together, about twenty tokens per parameter.
laws/under: G P T three had used fewer than two. It was under-trained.
laws/sizes: Models grew from millions of parameters to hundreds of billions, and training them became a field of its own.
rlhf/predictor: A pretrained model only predicts text. Ask it a question, and it may write three more.
rlhf/sft: So first it is fine-tuned on written examples of good answers.
rlhf/judge: But good answers are hard to write and easy to judge. So people compare two answers and pick the better one,
rlhf/rm: and a reward model learns to predict their choice.
rlhf/ppo: Then reinforcement learning, with P P O, pushes the model toward answers the reward model likes,
rlhf/kl: while a penalty keeps it close to where it started.
rlhf/instruct: That is R L H F. In twenty twenty two, people preferred a small Instruct G P T to a G P T three a hundred times its size.
rlhf/chatgpt: That November, Chat G P T, trained the same way, put it in front of everyone.
rlhf/dpo: In twenty twenty three, D P O did the same with one simple loss on the pairs: no reward model, no R L loop.
rlvr/hack: But a reward model is a learned guess, and a model optimized hard against it finds its blind spots: reward hacking.
rlvr/check: For math and code, we can do better: a program can check the answer.
rlvr/rlvr: Use the checker as the reward, and you have reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.
rlvr/grpo: G R P O, from DeepSeek in twenty twenty four, made it cheap. Sample a group of answers to one question,
rlvr/adv: and score each one against the group's average. Better than average is pushed up, worse is pushed down.
rlvr/o1: In September twenty twenty four, OpenAI's oh one was trained with R L to reason before answering, and got better the longer it thought.
rlvr/r1: In January twenty twenty five, DeepSeek R one published a recipe: with R L on checkable problems, long chains of reasoning grow on their own.
rlvr/grad: Under all of it is one update: the softmax gradient from C S two thirty one N, weighted by the reward.
carried/left: So what is left of C S two thirty one N? Almost everything underneath.
carried/step: Here is one training step of a language model today. Blue is what you already know; orange is new.
carried/back: Backpropagation computes every gradient, exactly as you did by hand.
carried/adam: An optimizer from the Adam family takes the step. AdamW only changes how weight decay is applied.
carried/loss: The loss is softmax cross-entropy, and the last layer is a linear classifier over the whole vocabulary.
carried/res: Every block adds its output back to its input: the residual connection from ResNet.
carried/norm: Normalization keeps the numbers in range, now per token, and weights still start small and random.
carried/new: What is new fits on one hand: tokens, positions and attention. That is where the course begins.
map/twenty: The course has twenty chapters after this one, in five parts that follow those threads.
map/p1: Attention and transformers: from recurrence to attention, the Transformer, tokens, and pretraining. Read these four first.
map/p2: Scale: scaling laws, the modern block, optimizers, training on many G P Us, and mixture of experts.
map/p3: Seeing and generating: vision transformers, clip, and diffusion.
map/p4: Post-training: fine-tuning, policy gradients, R L H F, D P O, G R P O and reasoning, best read in order.
map/p5: And serving and understanding: fast inference, and looking inside a model.
map/alone: Four chapters need only C S two thirty one N: tokens, optimizers, many G P Us, and diffusion.
map/recap: So: one architecture, scale as a plan, and learning from feedback, all built on tools you already have.
map/bet: And it all began with one bet, in twenty seventeen: that attention was all you need. Ten years on, the bet still stands.
